name: Multiband dynamics on a synth/pad bus: gentle low-band control, upward expand for weak lows, slow-attack top band
goal: Use a multiband compressor as a dynamic EQ rather than a squasher on a pad/synth or mix bus: enable only the band you need (e.g. low band below ~92 Hz with ~1.5 dB range, opto-style, fairly fast attack) to tame bass build-up, use expansion with a +dB band gain to make a weak low end bigger but cleaner, and use a slow attack on a top band so transients pass while splashy highs are controlled—then check tonal shift from the crossovers.

source.title: Ultimate Compression Tutorial Pt.5 - Multiband Compression quick settings for Drums and 2bus

prerequisites: Multiband compressor/expander with per-band bypass, solo, crossover, range/threshold, attack/release and band gain

inputs.name: crossover_hz
inputs.description: Band edge (example from transcript: 92 Hz for the low band)

outputs.name: bus_multiband_setup
outputs.description: Single-band (or few-band) dynamic control that leaves the rest of the spectrum untouched

constraints: Ground every step in the source YouTube-provided Show-transcript text; do not invent UI paths or numeric settings not stated there.
Original synthesis / signal-flow only — map brand UI to portable osc/filter/env/LFO/FX modules for Traveler-inspired or Web Audio hybrid; never rip presets, wavetables, or samples.
Not affiliated with the plugin/hardware vendors named in the source video; recreate with comparable modules.
Source examples are drum bus and full mix; applying to pad/synth buses is a portable transfer of the same band logic, not a claim from the video.
Portable alias: multiband compressor = crossover split + per-band compressor/expander + sum (Web Audio: biquad LR crossovers + DynamicsCompressorNode per band).
Delta vs midside-eq-bass-focus-width-depth and sidechain-compressor-duck-synth-pads: frequency-split dynamics, not static M/S EQ or kick-keyed ducking.

steps.action: Bypass all bands except the one covering the problem range; solo that band to hear exactly what it acts on.
steps.expect: Only the target range is processed

steps.action: Boomy lows: on the low band start aggressive to find it (e.g. -24 dB range, very fast attack), then ease off; a slower attack lets the initial transient/punch through and reduces the range after it, while a very fast attack chokes it.
steps.expect: Low end controlled without losing punch

steps.action: Real-world gentle setting: low band only, crossover ~92 Hz (acts like a dynamic low shelf), range ~1.5 dB, opto mode, fairly fast attack—'a couple of dB' makes a big difference.
steps.expect: Bass feels more controlled; change is subtle in A/B

steps.action: Weak lows: raise that band's gain (example +6 dB) and switch to expansion with lower threshold so the band stays down until a hit arrives, then returns to its boosted gain—cleaner low end between hits, bigger on hits.
steps.expect: Low band blooms on hits and recedes between them

steps.action: Harsh highs: on a top band use a slow attack so fast bright transients pass while sustained splashy energy is reduced; if it gets dark, add band gain to restore controlled brightness.

Set attack/release as with a wideband compressor: release roughly in time with the music and listen to the breathing. Use a band only for range problems that come and go (a static EQ handles constant ones).
A/B with the whole unit bypassed: splitting into bands with crossover filters shifts phase and tone even at zero gain reduction, so confirm the change is worth it.

verification: Gain reduction appears only on the enabled band
Low band shows ~1–3 dB reduction on loud passages, not constant heavy squash
Bypass A/B confirms improvement exceeds the crossover-induced tone shift
